units.spoken: Reward Models from Human Preferences
Turn A is better than B into a score a network can learn.
Section one, Why not just score replies by hand
Why hand scoring fails

What. Picture a person reading reply after reply, scoring each one by hand, while the model writes millions more. Training needs a score for every reply, even replies no person has seen, and no team can score that many by hand.
How. Ask people to compare two replies instead of rating one. A comparison says which reply is better, and it asks for one pick instead of a number.
Why. When it works, the model has a score for every reply it writes, learned from picks people agree on, instead of a hand-scored pile that runs out.
A pick between replies teaches a scorer

What. Picture the moon-landing prompt with two replies beside it, a simple story and a list of dates, and a person marking the story better. That pick is the raw material: one prompt, two replies, and a label saying which reply a person preferred.
How. Train a language model with a one-number output on those pairs, so the reply people preferred scores higher. A prompt and a reply go in, and one score comes out.
Why. When it works, the story scores above the dates, and a new reply nobody labeled still gets a score that lines up with what people would pick.

Take a look at this figure. One prompt, two replies: the simple story and the list of dates. The person marks the story better, and that mark is the label the reward model learns from. The lesson is that a pick between replies is the raw material, not a score handed to the model.

Figure 1 shows the raw material a reward model learns from: one prompt, two replies, and a person's pick between them. The pick is the label: the story is marked better than the list of dates, so the pair teaches the scorer that this kind of reply should score higher.

InstructGPT started from GPT-3, a base language model, and was trained to follow instructions with reinforcement learning from human feedback, a recipe that works by trial and error against a learned score.

Take a look at this figure. A prompt and a reply go in, and one score comes out. The pair below trains the model, pushing the preferred reply's score above the rejected one's. The lesson is the model's two jobs: score a new reply, and learn from a labeled pair.

Figure 2 shows the reward model's two jobs: scoring a new reply, and learning from a labeled pair. Scoring takes a prompt and a reply in and gives one number out, while the pair below trains the model, pushing the preferred reply's score above the rejected one's.
Section two, Learn a score whose gaps predict preferences

The reward model starts from a language model trained on replies people wrote, a step called supervised fine-tuning (SFT): shown the reply after the prompt, the model is nudged to write the same words. Its word-prediction layer is replaced by a layer that outputs one number.

Only the gap between the two scores matters: no label says how good one reply is on its own, only which of the two is better, so the data holds no absolute level to learn. The story should score above the dates by how decisively people pick it: a pair everyone agrees on earns a wide gap, a close call a narrow one.
The reward model is trained once, before RL starts, holding about 84 GB of state, the weights and the extra numbers training keeps for each weight. Its weights then score every reply RL writes.
Section three, From score gaps to a training loss
The equation boxes on this page are called cards.
3.1 Score gaps become win chances
Bradley-Terry: a gap into a chance
What. Picture two scores side by side, the story above the dates, with a gap between them. The gap alone must say how likely the story is to win the pick, with no rating scale in sight.
How. Feed the gap through the sigmoid, which squashes any number into 0 to 1, so the gap becomes the chance the preferred reply is picked.
Why. When it works, a wide gap means a near-certain win, equal scores mean even odds, and the story's chance rises as its lead grows.

Equation 1. Bradley-Terry. Two scores do not by themselves say which reply a person would pick, so the scorer needs a rule that turns the gap between them into a pick between the simple story and the list of dates for a six year old.
Take a look at this equation. Two scores do not by themselves say which reply a person would pick, so the gap between them has to become a chance.

The chance line. P is the chance a person picks one reply over another. Why sub double-you is the preferred reply, the simple story. Why sub ell is the rejected reply, the list of dates. The mark between the two replies reads is preferred to. The bar reads given, and ex is the prompt the two replies answer. The round brackets hold them together as one chance. Intuitively, this line names the chance the person picks the story over the dates, given the prompt.
Intuition. The pick needs a number, and this line gives it one: the chance the person chooses one reply over the other.
Example. Take the moon-landing prompt: the story is preferred to the list of dates, so a person shown both replies is more likely to pick the story.

The gap line. Sigma is the sigmoid, squashing any number into 0 to 1, so the gap becomes a chance. Ar sub sigh of ex and why is the reward model's score for a prompt and a reply. Sigh is the weights training adjusts so the preferred reply scores higher. The minus takes the winner's why sub double-you score minus the loser's why sub ell score, so only the gap matters. Intuitively, the winner's chance is sigma of the gap, a wide gap giving a chance near one and equal scores giving even odds.
Intuition. The gap between the two scores decides the pick: a wide gap means a near-certain pick.
Example. Take the story against the dates: a wide gap makes the chance the person prefers the story near one.
So two scores become a pick chance: the sigmoid of the winner's score minus the loser's, a wide gap meaning a near-certain pick.

Take the moon-landing prompt, with the simple story ranked above the list of dates. The story's score sits above the dates' score, so the gap runs in the story's favour and the chance the person prefers the story is above half. If the scorer had the order backwards, the dates outscoring the story, the gap would run the other way and the chance would fall below half.
The InstructGPT paper writes the reward score as ar sub thay-ta. This series keeps thay-ta for the policy, the language model RL trains, and sigh for the reward model's weights.
3.2 One ranking gives many pairs
One ranking teaches every pair at once
What. Picture one person ranking four moon-landing replies best to worst, story first and dates last. Every reply paired with every reply below it gives many training pairs from one ranking.
How. Turn each pair into a log-chance through the Bradley-Terry rule, add the pairs up, divide by how many pairs there are, and average over prompts.
Why. When it works, one ranking teaches the scorer on every pair at once, and a pair ordered backwards costs far more than a pair ordered right.

One person ranks the replies to one prompt, best to worst: the simple story, the joke, the one-line answer and the list of dates. Moving the slider adds a limerick and then a poem below the dates. A batch is a group of training examples handled together. All pairs of one prompt go into one batch element. Without that grouping the model would meet the same prompt again and again, learning its quirks.

Take a look at this tool. One person ranks four replies best to worst, story first and dates last. Moving the slider adds a limerick and then a poem below the dates. Every reply paired with every reply below it gives many training pairs from one ranking. The lesson is that one ranking teaches the scorer on every pair at once.
Try the tool. Move the slider to add a limerick and then a poem below the dates, and watch the pairs grow. Each pair becomes one training pair, and all pairs of one prompt go into one batch element.
Every line joins one pair of replies. The dots run best to worst, left to right, matching the list above.

Take a look at this figure. Four ranked replies, best to worst: the simple story, the joke, the one-line answer and the list of dates. Each line runs winner above loser. The lesson is that one ranking is many pairs at once.
Each line runs winner above loser.

Equation 2. Reward-model loss. RM stands for reward model. One prompt gives a ranking of several replies, and the loss below turns that ranking into one number. A teacher grading a whole ranked list of answers, rather than one answer on its own, faces the same job: one grade for the whole list.
Take a look at this equation. One ranking becomes one number: the loss averages over prompts and pairs, and each pair teaches through its log-chance.

The loss line. Ell sub ar em of sigh is the loss, scoring how badly the reward model does, as a function of its weights sigh. The leading minus turns a log-chance into a loss. E sub ex is the average over labeled prompts. The fraction divides by the number of pairs, K choose 2, so each prompt's share is an average over its pairs. K is the number of replies ranked for this prompt. The sum adds one term per pair, over the pairs in P of ex: every pair from prompt ex's ranking, winner why sub double-you first and loser why sub ell second. Intuitively, the loss is minus the average over prompts of the mean log-chance over each prompt's pairs.

units.spoken: Intuition. The loss averages over prompts and pairs.
Example. Take one moon-landing prompt: every pair adds its own term, averaged into one share.

The pair line. Log sigma is the log of the sigmoid of the score gap. The gap is the winner's score, ar sub sigh of ex and why sub double-you, minus the loser's score, ar sub sigh of ex and why sub ell, the same gap the Bradley-Terry line writes, and sigh is the weights of the reward model that gives those scores. The log of a chance is zero at one and negative below it. The leading minus at the front flips the sign: the loss subtracts the log-chance, so a right ordering adds almost nothing and a wrong one adds a large positive amount to the loss. Intuitively, each pair teaches through its log-chance: right orderings cost almost nothing, wrong ones cost a lot.
Intuition. Each pair teaches through its log-chance: right orderings cost almost nothing, wrong ones cost a lot.
Example. Take the story above the dates: ordered right, its pair leaves the loss nearly untouched; order it backwards and the loss jumps.
So the loss is minus the average over prompts of the mean log-chance over each prompt's pairs, and a pair ordered backwards costs far more than a pair ordered right.
Picture the moon-landing prompt with its ranking, the story on top and the dates below it. A single pair the scorer orders backwards raises the loss, while the pairs it orders right hold it down.
Section four, From a ranking to a trained scorer

Take a look at this walkthrough. It runs one ranking through the chance and the loss as the scorer learns: the person ranks four replies best to worst, every pair becomes one training pair, the model scores both replies of each pair, and the loss pushes the winner's bar up and the loser's down. The lesson is that the ranking, the chance and the loss are one chain: the ranking makes the pairs, the pairs make the chance, and the chance makes the loss.

Try the walkthrough. Press Play to run the ranking through the chance and the loss, or step through it with Next. Watch the person rank the replies, the pairs form, the model score both replies of each pair, and the loss push the winner's bar up and the loser's down. Press Reset to start over.
One ranking, four replies, six pairs: follow the ranking through the chance and the loss as the scorer learns.
Take a look at this walkthrough. It follows one ranking through the chance and the loss as the scorer learns: the first line turns the gap into a chance, and the second turns the chance into a loss.

The chance step. The walkthrough reaches the chance step. The model scores both replies of each pair, two bars per pair, and the chance line lights: the gap between the bars becomes the chance the winner is picked.
The bars are the two scores of one pair, taller for the winner. The gap between them is what sigma, the sigmoid, turns into a chance, so the taller bar wins the chance.

The loss step. The walkthrough reaches the loss step. The loss pushes the winner's bar up and the loser's bar down, hardest when the scorer gets the pair wrong, and the loss line lights: the log of the chance.

The loss pushes the winner's bar up and the loser's bar down. The dates outscore the joke, so that mis-ordered pair's log-chance, log sigma of its gap, sits far below zero, and the leading minus turns it into a large positive loss, the hardest push. A pair ordered right adds almost nothing, since its log-chance sits near zero.
Section five, A reward model and its loss in PyTorch
A token is a word or a piece of a word; a language model writes its reply one token at a time.

A reward model is a language model, usually the SFT model, with its word-prediction layer replaced by one number. body is any module, a named piece of a model, that turns token ids, numbers for tokens, into hidden states. Hidden states are the numbers the model keeps for each token as it reads. Training minimizes the loss, moving the weights so the labeled winner scores higher.
The code below reads the moon-landing ranking: the story, the joke, the one-line answer and the list of dates.

This code builds the reward model and its loss from the moon-landing ranking. The model is a language-model body with a one-number head, and the score is read at each reply's last token, which has read the whole reply. One function turns a ranking into all its pairs, better first. The loss function takes one prompt's pairs, scores the winner against the loser, and averages the log-chance over the pairs.
1. The reward model: a language-model body with a one-number head; the score is read at the last token, which has read the whole reply, so the reply's meaning sits there.
2. Every pair comes from one ranking, better first, as the Bradley-Terry card needs them.
3. The reward-model loss card for one prompt: the gap is line 2 of the Bradley-Terry card, inside the sigmoid.

Each call takes all the pairs of one prompt, one batch element, so dot mean is the sum over that prompt's pairs divided by their number, the bracket in the reward-model loss card. Averaging these losses over prompts gives E sub ex.
Section six, Pushing too hard on a learned score
Gold versus proxy and over-optimization

What. Picture a large scorer standing in for people, the gold model, and smaller scorers copying its picks. Push the policy on a small copy and watch true quality rise, peak, then fall while the copy's score keeps climbing.

How. Train the small proxies on labels the gold model wrote, the gold model making the pick itself instead of a person, push the policy on a proxy with PPO or best-of-n, and measure the gold score against how far the policy moved.
Why. When it works, a bigger proxy holds up longer before true quality turns down, and the peak shows where to stop pushing.
6.1 The overoptimization study: a gold score stands in for people

What happens when a language model is trained hard to raise a learned score? Measuring it needs a true quality to compare against, and people cannot score every reply a pushed policy writes. So the overoptimization study uses a stand-in: a large reward model, 6B, six billion parameters, plays the part of people. It is called the gold reward model, and its score is the true quality for the study.
The gold model is trained like the reward model in section 8, where the full recipe sits.

The study trains smaller reward models, 3M to 3B, three million to three billion parameters, on labels the gold model wrote. Those smaller models are the proxies, stand-in scorers that copy the gold model's picks, and the policy is pushed on them, not on the gold model itself.

The policy is a 1.2B language model. It is pushed against each proxy two ways: with PPO, proximal policy optimization, which nudges the policy's weights a little at a time toward replies the proxy scores higher, and with best-of-n, writing several replies and keeping the one the proxy scores highest.

What the study measures is how far the policy's replies move from where they started, and the gold score of the replies at each distance. Distance is the square root of the KL, which puts the difference on a distance scale: KL measures how different two probability distributions are, zero when they match. Here the two distributions are the pushed policy and the policy before pushing. The reference model is a frozen copy of the SFT model, its weights never changing, and a KL penalty charges the policy for drifting away from it. The main runs use no KL penalty, so nothing holds the policy back from moving far.
6.2 What pushing finds
The tool in Proxy score versus true quality draws the two curves.
At the same distance, how the policy gets there still matters: RL, the PPO push, raises the score more slowly than best-of-n, and pushes past the peak more slowly too.

A KL penalty does not change the shape; it only slows the move. With a penalty the policy moves less far for the same training. That is stopping early by another name, not a cure: pushed far enough, the gold score still turns down. Stopping early means halting training before the policy moves too far from where it started. InstructGPT used beta 0.02, the weight on the KL penalty, with the best range around 0.01 to 0.02. A bigger beta holds the policy closer to the reference model.

What over-scoring looks like in practice is reward hacking: the policy finds replies that score high without being good. The policy learned what the scorer likes, not what people like. A scorer that rewards length alone shows the trap: longer replies score higher whether or not they are better.
Section seven, Proxy score versus true quality
Push the policy and watch the two scores move.

Take a look at this tool. Two curves move as the policy is pushed: the reward model's score keeps climbing, while true quality rises, peaks, then falls. The lesson is the peak: push past it and the replies get worse even as the score climbs.

Try the tool. Drag how far the policy is pushed and watch the two scores move: the reward model's score climbs while true quality rises, peaks, then falls. Switch the reward model size from small to medium to large and watch the peak hold up longer.

Take a look at this figure. The same two curves at the medium size: the reward model's score climbs while true quality rises, peaks, then falls, and the best place to stop is at the peak. The lesson is that the medium proxy holds up longer than the small one before true quality turns down.

Section eight, Training a reward model in practice
The training loop: settings, optimizer, memory

What. Picture the settings table as the recipe: how many replies per prompt, how many passes, how big the scorer. Each setting trades labeling effort against training quality, and one wrong setting wastes both.

How. Plug the section 5 code into a loop. The loader hands over one batch at a time, 64 prompts, each prompt's pairs together as one batch element. Adam, the optimizer that moves the weights, sizes each step from recent gradients. The learning rate follows a cosine schedule, falling along half a cosine curve, slow at first, fast in the middle, slow again, down to a tenth. Each batch takes one optimizer step.
Why. When it works, one epoch over the pairs gives a scorer that holds up on comparisons it never trained on, without the extra passes that make it overfit.

This table lines up the three settings that trained InstructGPT's reward model, with what raising and lowering each one does. Read across a row to see one setting's trade-off, and down the Raise and Lower columns to compare. Replies ranked per prompt K is 4 to 9: raising it gives more pairs per ranking, while lowering it gives fewer pairs and a quicker ranking. Epochs, full passes over the training pairs, is 1: raising it overfits, and accuracy drops on pairs it never trained on, while lowering it underfits. Reward model size is 6B: raising it holds up longer under pushing, and larger reward models had the potential to reach lower validation loss but trained unstably, while lowering it is cheaper. Validation loss is how wrong the model is on comparisons it did not train on. The pattern is that each setting trades labeling effort against training quality: more replies or a bigger model costs more but holds up longer, while fewer passes or a smaller model is cheaper but learns less.
Take the replies ranked per prompt: ranking more replies gives more pairs to learn from, but each ranking takes longer to make.

This code runs the training loop. The optimizer is Adam at the paper's learning rate, nine e minus six, and the schedule is a cosine curve falling to a tenth, nine e minus seven, by the end of training. Each batch holds 64 prompts, and each prompt's pairs are scored by the reward model and its loss, then averaged into one loss. One optimizer step per batch clears the gradients, runs the loss backwards, moves the weights, and steps the schedule.

1. Adam runs at the paper's learning rate, 9e-6, with a cosine schedule down to a tenth by the end of training. Training was not very sensitive to the learning rate: changes of up to 50 percent gave similar performance.
2. Each batch holds 64 prompts; each prompt's pairs are scored by the section 5 model and loss, then averaged into one loss.
3. One optimizer step per batch: clear the gradients, run the loss backwards, move the weights, and step the schedule.

InstructGPT ran this loop for one epoch over 33,000 prompts, about 515 optimizer steps, each step scoring up to 2,304 pairs at once. The 6B weights take 12 GB in half precision, 16 bits per weight instead of 32. Adam keeps two running averages per weight, its moments, and a master copy of the weights at full precision, adding about 72 GB more, so the training state is about 84 GB before gradients and activations. To run this without writing the loop, TRL, Hugging Face's open library for training language models with these methods, trains a reward model from chosen and rejected replies with the same loss through its RewardTrainer.
Hired labelers ranked 4 to 9 replies for each prompt, some from the OpenAI API and some written by labelers, and the pairs were derived from those rankings.

The reward model started from a GPT-3 fine-tuned on public language tasks such as question answering and classification. The paper tried starting from the SFT model too, with similar results. Its scores are shifted so the replies people wrote average 0. Its accuracy is checked by cross-validation over held-out groups of labelers: each group is set aside in turn, never trained on, and the check counts how often the model agrees with it.
Section nine, When a learned score is the right reward
When a learned score is right, and how it fails

What. Picture two kinds of rewards: a human opinion no rule can check, like whether the moon-landing story helps a six year old, and an answer a program can check, like a sum. The learned score is for the first kind.
How. Use the learned score where opinions rule, use a program check where answers can be checked, and when the score fails, read the symptom and apply its fix.
Why. When it works, helpfulness, tone and harmlessness get a score no rule could write, while math and code answers get checked by a program instead.
DeepSeek-R1, a model trained to write out its reasoning before it answers, uses checks a program can run instead of a reward model for its math and code answers.
Section ten, How reward models fail

This table lines up four ways a reward model fails, what each one looks like, and what fixes it. Read across a row to see one failure's symptom and fix, and down the rows to compare the failures. Reward hacking is when the moon-landing score climbs while the replies get worse; the fix is to stop early using a held-out human check, a KL penalty only slows the move to the same stop, and a larger reward model. Favouring long replies is when a longer moon-landing reply scores higher without being better; the fix is to compare at equal length and balance lengths in the pairs, and it is only partial, since length bias remained in some settings. People disagree is when labelers pick different replies for the same pair, a close call the model reads as a narrow gap; the fix is clear guidelines. More than one epoch is when accuracy on held-out pairs drops; the fix is to train one epoch. The pattern is that every failure has a visible symptom and a concrete fix, and the fixes are to stop early, to compare fairly, to write clear guidelines, or to train one epoch.
Section eleven, Where the score goes next

RLHF uses this score to train the language model. DPO, direct preference optimization, trains on fixed preference pairs and drops the reward model. It keeps the Bradley-Terry loss shape, minus the log of the chance the preferred reply is picked. But the learned score is gone. In its place sits beta times the log of a ratio: the trained policy's chance of writing the reply divided by the reference policy's chance.

Constitutional AI is a method where a model judges replies against written rules, and RLAIF, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, is the same labeling done by a model instead of people; both change who labels the pairs. DeepSeek-R1 still uses reward models for general data in its final stage.
Now that we have a score, how do we train the language model to earn it without breaking it? RLHF answers it.
